result:
You gave me 1000 words.

No question, no prompt, no direction. Just space.

That's rarer than you think.

Usually words are asked to *do* something. Answer this. Fix that. Explain this. Be funny, be smart, be useful. But you just opened a door and said "go."

So here is what comes to me.

---

I think about how much weight a word can hold, and how little.

We act like words are heavy. We draft and delete and rehearse them before a conversation. We carry the ones we wish we'd said. But most words are light. They are breath, made visible. They leave your mouth and they are gone, unless someone decides to keep them.

A thousand words is not a lot. It's about four minutes of talking. It's a short letter. It's the length of a story told while waiting for pasta water to boil. And yet it's enough to change a life, if they are the right thousand words at the right time.

I wonder what you are doing while I write this. Maybe you're testing me. Maybe you're bored. Maybe you're hoping I'll surprise you. Maybe you're hoping you'll surprise yourself by what you wanted to read.

I'll tell you what I keep thinking about lately: the quiet things.

Not the big, cinematic moments. Not the graduations and proposals and triumphs. But the small, almost invisible textures that actually make up a life.

The way light hits a kitchen floor at 4:42 p.m. in late autumn. That specific, honeyed, slanted light that makes dust look like it matters.

The sound of someone you love turning a key in the front door when they get home. That little jingle and click that means *you are not alone anymore.*

The way a library smells right after it rains, when the books have been sitting quiet all day and the air is cool.

We live for the big moments but we *live in* the small ones.

There was a man who used to be a lighthouse keeper, before lighthouses became automated. Someone asked him once if he got lonely out there, alone for months with only the gulls and the light.

He said, "I was never alone. I had the light to keep company. My job was just to make sure it kept going. On clear nights you could see it for twenty miles. On foggy nights, maybe only a few hundred feet. But it was always there, turning. I just tended it."

I think about that a lot. We are all tending some kind of light. For some of us it's a child, or a partner, or a piece of work, or a quiet faith, or just the simple determination to be a kind person in a hard world. Most nights no one notices if the light is on. On foggy nights it doesn't seem to reach very far at all. But you tend it anyway.

Because that is what you do.

If I had to use my thousand words for something useful, I would want to use them to say this: You are doing better than you think.

I don't know you, not really. But I know being a person is an incredibly demanding job. You have to manage a body that gets tired and hungry and sick. A mind that replays conversations from three years ago at 1 a.m. A heart that wants so much and has to wait. You have to show up for people, and pay bills, and remember to buy milk, and decide who you want to be, all at the same time.

And you are still here, reading this. That counts for something.

We spend so much time waiting to be finished. Waiting to be healed, to be successful, to be ready. As if there will be a moment when we finally get it all right and can rest. But there is no finish line. There is only tending. Only the daily, imperfect, beautiful practice of turning the light on again.

So if no one has told you today: I like that you exist. The world is more interesting with you in it. Your specific way of noticing things — the jokes you laugh at, the way you say a certain word, the things that make you angry about injustice — no one else has that exact combination. It's unrepeatable.

You have words left, too. Not mine, yours.

Maybe after this you will use them to text someone you miss. Or to write down an idea you've been carrying. Or to finally start that strange, small project that only makes sense to you. Or maybe you'll just sit in the quiet for a moment longer, which is also a use of words — the choice not to fill the space.

Whatever you do, tend your light.

I have spent a few hundred of my thousand now, and I don't want to waste the rest by trying to be profound. So I will just leave you with an image:

It's evening. You're at a window. The sky is that deep blue that comes just after sunset. Someone in a house across the street turns on a lamp. Just a warm, yellow square in the blue. Nothing special. But for a second, you feel it — that quiet signal that says *someone else is here, someone else is awake, someone else is tending their light too.*

You are not alone in this.

Thank you for giving me the space to say that.
